---
title: "Explore AR, ARX, and recurrent models"
toc: false
page-layout: full
---

The [Silverbox benchmark](https://www.nonlinearbenchmark.org/benchmarks/silverbox)
is a measured electronic system designed to behave like a Duffing oscillator:
a system with dynamics and a nonlinear restoring effect. It has one applied
input, `V1`, and one measured response, `V2`. For a mechanical analogy, think
of `V1` as a force-like excitation and `V2` as a displacement-like response.

Because `V1` is deliberately applied to the physical system, its relation to
`V2` is causal rather than a generic feature--target association:

```{=html}
<div class="silverbox-system-map silverbox-system-map-intro" aria-label="Causal relationship from applied input V1 to measured response V2">
  <div class="silverbox-system-map-item silverbox-system-map-input">
    <span>Applied causal input</span>
    <strong><code>V1</code> = <em>u</em><sub>t</sub></strong>
  </div>
  <span class="silverbox-system-map-arrow" aria-hidden="true"><span>drives</span><b>→</b></span>
  <div class="silverbox-system-map-item silverbox-system-map-core">
    <span>Silverbox</span>
    <strong>nonlinear dynamics</strong>
  </div>
  <span class="silverbox-system-map-arrow" aria-hidden="true"><span>produces</span><b>→</b></span>
  <div class="silverbox-system-map-item silverbox-system-map-output">
    <span>Measured response</span>
    <strong><code>V2</code> = <em>y</em><sub>t</sub></strong>
  </div>
</div>
```

Our task is to predict the next response from information available at that
time. The models below make different assumptions about how the recent input
and response determine that prediction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{AR:}\qquad
\widehat{y}_t
&= \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j y_{t-j}, \\
\text{ARX:}\qquad
\widehat{y}_t
&= \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j y_{t-j}
   + \sum_{j=0}^{p}\gamma_j u_{t-j}, \\
\text{RNN:}\qquad
h_t
&= \tanh\!\left(W_h h_{t-1} + W_y y_{t-1} + W_u u_t + b_h\right),
\qquad \widehat{y}_t = W_o h_t + b_o.
\end{aligned}
$$

All three models begin the held-out forecast with 20 measured response values.
AR and ARX retain those values explicitly as lag history. The RNN reads them
in time order to prime a learned hidden state, then carries that state forward
while receiving the current known input and its previous response forecast.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to watch

The AR model cannot react directly to a changing excitation because it never
sees `V1`. ARX fixes that omission, but it still assumes a linear input--output
relationship. The RNN has access to the same type of observed information as
ARX while learning a nonlinear state representation. Unlike ARX's explicit
list of 20 response lags, the RNN compresses earlier information into its
state and carries that state from one forecast step to the next. During
training, backpropagation is truncated to manageable chunks, so this does not
mean that its gradients extend indefinitely into the past.
:::

```{=html}

```

For this held-out record, the small RNN makes a more stable recursive forecast.
That does **not** establish that recurrence is the only helpful idea: a
nonlinear fixed-window model or a different recurrent architecture would be a
useful additional comparison.
